questions.stem: The psychometric approach to intelligence is best described as:
options: describing the mental steps a person uses to solve a novel problem
observing how intelligence develops through stages in childhood
explaining intelligence as several independent abilities of equal worth
measuring differences in intelligence with standardised tests
questions.explanation: Psychometrics is the measurement of psychological traits, so the psychometric approach uses standardised tests to give each person a score, usually an IQ, that can be compared with others. Describing the mental steps used in problem solving is the information processing approach.

questions.stem: In the psychometric approach, what does an intelligence quotient (IQ) score show?
options: How a person's performance compares with others of the same age
The total number of test items a person answered correctly overall
The amount of intelligence a person inherited from their parents
How quickly a person's intelligence will develop in the future
questions.explanation: Modern IQ scores compare an individual's performance with a norm group of the same age, so 100 is average for that age. A raw score is just the number correct, and an IQ says nothing about how much of a person's intelligence was inherited.

questions.stem: Under the original ratio formula, IQ = mental age / chronological age × 100. A 10-year-old performs at the level of a typical 12-year-old. What is the child's IQ?
questions.explanation: IQ = 12 / 10 × 100 = 120. Dividing chronological age by mental age instead gives 10 / 12 × 100, about 83, which would wrongly suggest below-average performance.

questions.stem: Why did modern IQ tests replace the ratio IQ (mental age / chronological age × 100) with a deviation IQ?
options: Mental age can be measured only in adults, so the ratio could not be used for children
The ratio formula gave every person of the same age exactly the same score
Mental age stops increasing in adulthood, so the ratio makes no sense for adults
The ratio formula could only be calculated for people with above-average ability
questions.explanation: Performance on test items levels off in early adulthood, so a 40-year-old with an adult's mental age would get an ever-falling ratio IQ just by ageing. A deviation IQ compares a person with others their own age, which works at any age.

questions.stem: On modern deviation IQ scales such as the Wechsler scales, scores are standardised to have:
options: a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 10
a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 15
a mean of 115 and a standard deviation of 15
a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15
questions.explanation: Deviation IQs are set so the average for each age group is 100 and the standard deviation is 15. A score of 115 is therefore one standard deviation above the mean, not the mean itself.

questions.stem: IQ scores are normally distributed with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. About what percentage of people score between 85 and 115?
questions.explanation: 85 and 115 are one standard deviation either side of the mean, and about 68% of a normal distribution lies within one standard deviation. About 95% lies within two standard deviations (70 to 130), and 34% is the share on just one side of the mean.

questions.stem: IQ scores are normally distributed with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. About what percentage of people score above 130?
questions.explanation: About 95% of scores lie within two standard deviations, between 70 and 130, leaving 5% split equally between the two tails, so about 2.5% score above 130. About 16% score above 115, one standard deviation above the mean.

questions.stem: Alfred Binet and Theodore Simon developed the first practical intelligence test in France in the early 1900s. What was it designed to do?
options: Select the most capable adults for officer training in the army
Measure the separate intelligences described by multiple intelligence theory
Show that intelligence is fixed at birth and passed on through families
Identify schoolchildren who needed extra help with their learning
questions.explanation: Binet and Simon were asked to find a way to identify children who would struggle in ordinary classes and needed extra support. Their test was later revised at Stanford University by Lewis Terman to become the Stanford-Binet scale.

questions.stem: The WISC-V and the WAIS-IV are both Wechsler intelligence scales. How do they differ?
options: The WISC-V is a group test and the WAIS-IV is given one person at a time
The WISC-V is designed for children and the WAIS-IV for adults
The WISC-V is designed for adults and the WAIS-IV for children
The WISC-V measures emotional intelligence and the WAIS-IV measures IQ
questions.explanation: WISC stands for Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children and WAIS for Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale. Both are given individually by a trained tester and give a full scale IQ along with index scores.

questions.stem: Besides a full scale IQ, the WAIS-IV reports index scores such as verbal comprehension, working memory and processing speed. What is the main advantage of these index scores?
options: They make the test equally valid for people from every culture and language
They measure creative and practical abilities that the full scale IQ ignores
They show a profile of a person's relative strengths and weaknesses
They remove any need for the test to be given by a trained psychologist
questions.explanation: Index scores break overall performance into areas, so two people with the same full scale IQ can show very different profiles, which is useful for identifying learning difficulties. They do not remove cultural bias, and they still measure analytical abilities rather than Sternberg's creative and practical intelligence.

questions.stem: A psychologist gives a 9-year-old an intelligence test one-on-one, with set instructions, timing and scoring, and compares his result with a large sample of 9-year-olds tested earlier. The large sample provides the test's:
options: reliability
operational definition
validity
norms
questions.explanation: Norms are the scores of a large representative standardisation sample, against which an individual's score is compared. Reliability is the consistency of a test's results and validity is whether it measures what it claims to measure.

questions.stem: Why are standardised procedures (the same instructions, timing and scoring for everyone) important when giving the Stanford-Binet or a Wechsler scale?
options: They guarantee the test is free of any cultural bias against minority groups
They allow the tester to change questions to suit each person's interests
They make sure every person tested will receive a score close to 100
Score differences then reflect the people, not how the test was run
questions.explanation: If everyone is tested in the same way, a difference between two scores can be attributed to the test-takers rather than to the conditions, and scores can be compared fairly with the norms. Standardised procedures do not remove bias built into the content of the items.

questions.stem: The information processing approach to intelligence focuses on:
options: mental processes such as processing speed and working memory
ranking people by a single score compared with others of the same age
the different cultural settings in which practical intelligence is valued
the number of separate intelligences each person shows in daily life
questions.explanation: The information processing approach treats the mind like a system that takes in, stores and manipulates information, and asks how efficiently people do this, for example how fast they process information and how much they can hold in working memory. Ranking people by a single score is the psychometric approach.

questions.stem: In a study, participants who could identify a briefly flashed shape at shorter display times tended to score higher on IQ tests. This finding best supports:
options: the information processing approach
Gardner's multiple intelligences
Goleman's emotional intelligence
Sternberg's practical intelligence
questions.explanation: Measures of how quickly a person can take in simple information, such as inspection time and reaction time, are information processing measures, and a link with IQ suggests speed of processing contributes to intelligence. Gardner's theory is about distinct abilities such as musical or interpersonal intelligence, not processing speed.

questions.stem: How does the information processing approach differ most clearly from the psychometric approach?
options: It rejects the use of any quantitative measurement in the study of intelligence
It argues that intelligence is entirely inherited rather than shaped by experience
It ranks people against others of the same age using a deviation IQ score
It explains how a person reaches answers, not just how many are right
questions.explanation: The psychometric approach measures what a person can do and compares scores, whereas the information processing approach studies the mental processes, such as encoding, strategies and speed, behind performance. It still measures things quantitatively, for example reaction times.

questions.stem: Which three abilities make up Sternberg's triarchic theory of intelligence?
options: Analytical, creative and practical
Verbal, numerical and spatial
Linguistic, musical and naturalistic
Self-awareness, empathy and social skill
questions.explanation: Sternberg proposed analytical intelligence (solving familiar problems), creative intelligence (dealing with new situations) and practical intelligence (adapting to everyday settings). Self-awareness, empathy and social skill are parts of Goleman's emotional intelligence.

questions.stem: Kai left school early but runs a successful small business, reading customers well and solving everyday problems quickly, although he scores only average on IQ tests. Sternberg would say Kai shows high:
options: intrapersonal intelligence
practical intelligence
analytical intelligence
creative intelligence
questions.explanation: Practical intelligence is the ability to adapt to, shape and select real-world environments, often called street smarts, and it is poorly measured by IQ tests. Analytical intelligence is the kind IQ tests mostly measure, so it does not explain Kai's average score.

questions.stem: A designer quickly invents an original solution to a problem nobody in her team has met before. In Sternberg's triarchic theory, this shows:
options: logical-mathematical intelligence
creative intelligence
analytical intelligence
practical intelligence
questions.explanation: Creative intelligence is the ability to deal with novel situations and generate new ideas. Analytical intelligence is about evaluating and solving problems with known methods, and logical-mathematical intelligence belongs to Gardner's theory, not Sternberg's.

questions.stem: Sternberg argued that traditional IQ tests mainly assess only one part of intelligence. Which part, and what does this imply?
options: Practical intelligence, so IQ alone may overestimate people who do well in everyday situations
Creative intelligence, so IQ alone may underestimate people strong in school-type reasoning
Emotional intelligence, so IQ alone may overestimate people who manage relationships well
Analytical intelligence, so IQ may underestimate people strong in creative or practical skills
questions.explanation: IQ tests largely assess analytical, school-type problem solving with one right answer. Sternberg argued this misses creative and practical intelligence, so someone with an average IQ may still succeed through those abilities.

questions.stem: Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences proposes that:
options: intelligence is made up of three processes: analytical, creative and practical
a single general factor underlies performance on every type of mental task
intelligence is best measured by how quickly a person processes information
people have several relatively independent intelligences, not one
questions.explanation: Gardner argued for a set of distinct intelligences, such as linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal and naturalist. The three processes analytical, creative and practical are Sternberg's triarchic theory.

questions.stem: A student easily senses how others are feeling and is skilled at working in teams. In Gardner's theory, this is:
options: intrapersonal intelligence
naturalist intelligence
linguistic intelligence
interpersonal intelligence
questions.explanation: Interpersonal intelligence is understanding and relating to other people. Intrapersonal intelligence is the easily confused term for understanding yourself: your own feelings, motives and goals.

questions.stem: A surgeon has excellent fine control of her hands and an athlete has precise control of whole-body movement. Which of Gardner's intelligences do both show?
options: Naturalist
Logical-mathematical
Bodily-kinaesthetic
Spatial
questions.explanation: Bodily-kinaesthetic intelligence is skilled control of body movements and handling objects. Spatial intelligence is the ability to perceive and mentally manipulate visual and spatial information, as an architect or navigator does.

questions.stem: Which is the most common scientific criticism of Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences?
options: Little empirical evidence shows the intelligences are separate and measurable
It defines intelligence too narrowly by focusing on analytical school skills
It relies too heavily on standardised tests that produce a single IQ score
It has been shown that each intelligence is controlled by a single gene
questions.explanation: Gardner's intelligences are hard to measure, and critics argue there is little evidence that they are independent; some say abilities such as musical skill are talents rather than intelligences. The theory is criticised for being too broad, not too narrow, and Gardner did not develop standardised IQ-type tests for it.

questions.stem: Many teachers like Gardner's theory. What is its main appeal in education?
options: It proves that every student learns best in one fixed learning style
It values abilities IQ tests ignore, such as musical and interpersonal skills
It provides a single reliable score for placing students into ability groups
It shows that intelligence cannot be changed by teaching or experience
questions.explanation: The theory encourages teachers to recognise and develop a broad range of abilities rather than only verbal and mathematical skills. It does not give a single score, and multiple intelligences should not be confused with the idea of learning styles, which is not well supported.

questions.stem: Goleman's concept of emotional intelligence (EQ) refers to:
options: the strength of a person's autonomic arousal when they feel an emotion
the ability to solve abstract problems while under emotional pressure
the ability to recognise and manage your own emotions and those of others
the speed with which a person processes emotional information in the brain
questions.explanation: Emotional intelligence is about perceiving, understanding and managing emotions in yourself and in relationships. Goleman popularised the idea and described components such as self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills.

questions.stem: A team leader notices she is becoming angry in a meeting, takes a breath and responds calmly. In Goleman's model of emotional intelligence, she is showing:
options: interpersonal intelligence
self-regulation
empathy
social skills
questions.explanation: Self-regulation is controlling and redirecting disruptive emotions and impulses. Empathy is understanding other people's feelings, which is about others rather than managing her own anger.

questions.stem: Emotional intelligence is often measured with self-report questionnaires. Why does this weaken the validity of many EQ measures?
options: Self-report questionnaires cannot be given to more than one person at a time
Self-report questionnaires measure processing speed rather than emotions
Self-report questionnaires always give different results each time they are used
People may lack insight into their emotional skills or present themselves well
questions.explanation: A person who rates themselves as highly empathic may not be, either through poor self-insight or a wish to look good (social desirability), so the score may not measure actual emotional ability. Critics also note that many EQ measures overlap heavily with personality traits.

questions.stem: Students who took an IQ test twice, six weeks apart, received very similar scores both times. This shows the test has good:
options: external validity
test-retest reliability
predictive validity
content validity
questions.explanation: Reliability is consistency, and test-retest reliability is shown when the same people get similar scores on two occasions. Consistent scores do not show that the test measures intelligence, which is a question of validity.

questions.stem: IQ scores at age 10 are moderately correlated with later school results. This is evidence that IQ tests have some:
options: internal consistency
predictive validity
test-retest reliability
inter-rater reliability
questions.explanation: Predictive validity is the extent to which a test predicts a future outcome it should be related to, such as academic achievement. Reliability concerns consistency of scores, not whether they predict anything.

questions.stem: A test of 'general knowledge' asks city children and children from a remote community about tram timetables and supermarket layouts. The remote community children score lower. What best explains this?
options: The test is culturally biased: it measures familiarity with city life
The test is unreliable, so the scores would change if it were given a second time
The test has good validity, so the difference must reflect a real gap in intelligence
The test is standardised, so any difference in scores must be due to inherited ability
questions.explanation: Items that depend on experiences more common in one group favour that group, so a lower score can reflect less exposure to the content rather than lower ability. This is a validity problem, because the test is not measuring what it claims to; a biased test can still give very consistent results.

questions.stem: Raven's Progressive Matrices uses non-verbal patterns rather than words or general knowledge. Why do test developers use items like these?
options: To reduce the influence of language and cultural knowledge on scores
To measure emotional intelligence rather than general mental ability
To make sure the test can only be completed by adults, not children
To measure creative intelligence by having no single correct answer
questions.explanation: Abstract pattern items are designed to rely less on vocabulary and culturally specific knowledge, so they are described as culture-reduced. Even so, familiarity with this kind of puzzle and with testing itself can still affect scores, so no test is completely culture-free.

questions.stem: Raw scores on IQ tests rose steadily across the 20th century in many countries, so tests had to be re-normed. Why does this rise suggest environmental influences on IQ?
options: It proves that the heritability of intelligence in a population is zero
A population's genes cannot change fast enough to explain the rise
It shows that IQ tests were unreliable before they were re-normed each time
It shows that intelligence is fixed at birth and cannot be changed by experience
questions.explanation: The gene pool of a population changes far too slowly to produce large gains in a few decades, so changes such as better nutrition, schooling and familiarity with tests are more plausible explanations. This does not mean genes play no role: genes can explain differences between people within a generation while the environment shifts the whole distribution.

questions.stem: Why are identical (monozygotic) twins useful in studies of the inheritance of intelligence?
options: They share all their genes, so differences between them reflect environment
They always grow up in identical environments, so differences must be genetic
They share about half their genes, the same as any pair of ordinary siblings
They have identical IQ scores, which shows intelligence is completely inherited
questions.explanation: Monozygotic twins develop from one fertilised egg and are genetically identical, so differences between them reflect environmental factors. Fraternal (dizygotic) twins share on average about half their genes, like ordinary siblings.

questions.stem: In a twin study, identical twins' IQ scores are more strongly correlated than fraternal twins' scores, even though both kinds of twin pairs were raised together. What does this suggest?
options: Fraternal twins grow up in more varied homes than identical twins
Intelligence is determined by a single inherited gene
Genes contribute to differences in intelligence
The environment has no influence on intelligence
questions.explanation: Both types of twins share their family environment, but identical twins share more genes, so their greater similarity points to a genetic contribution. It does not show the environment has no effect, because identical twins' IQs are still not perfectly correlated.

questions.stem: In an adoption study, adopted children's IQ scores are compared with those of their biological parents and their adoptive parents. If the children's IQs correlate more strongly with their biological parents, this suggests:
options: an environmental influence on intelligence
that the adoptive homes were all identical
that the tests used were culturally biased
a genetic influence on intelligence
questions.explanation: Biological parents contribute genes but, after adoption, not the child's environment, while adoptive parents provide the environment but not genes. A stronger link with biological parents points to genetic influence; a stronger link with adoptive parents would point to the environment.

questions.stem: The Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart (Bouchard and colleagues, 1990) studied identical twins separated early in life and raised in different homes. Why are such twins especially informative?
options: They share about half of their genes, which allows genes to be measured directly
They were randomly allocated to homes chosen to be as different as possible
Similarities between them cannot be explained by sharing the same family home
Differences between them cannot be explained by any environmental factor at all
questions.explanation: Identical twins raised apart share all their genes but not their family environment, so their similarity in IQ is strong evidence of genetic influence. However, they were not randomly allocated to homes; adoptive homes are often similar, and the twins shared a prenatal environment, which limits the conclusions.

questions.stem: Read these correlations of IQ scores from a hypothetical family study: identical twins raised together 0.85; identical twins raised apart 0.75; fraternal twins raised together 0.60; unrelated children raised together 0.25. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Both genes and environment influence intelligence
Intelligence is determined only by genes
Intelligence is determined only by the environment
Shared family environment has no effect on intelligence
questions.explanation: Greater genetic similarity goes with higher correlations (identical above fraternal), which points to genes; but identical twins raised together are more alike than those raised apart, and unrelated children raised together still correlate, which points to the environment. Together the data support an interaction of both.

questions.stem: A report says the heritability of intelligence in a population is high. A student concludes that her own IQ was mostly set by her genes. Why is her conclusion wrong?
options: Heritability describes the variation across a population, not the causes in one person
Heritability applies only to identical twins, not to people who are not twins
Heritability is a measure of reliability, so it shows only that IQ tests are consistent
Heritability is always zero for individuals who were raised by their biological parents
questions.explanation: A heritability estimate is the proportion of the differences between people in a particular population and environment that is associated with genetic differences. It cannot be applied to one person, and it can change if the environment changes.
